Case Vignette: Raj, Age 29

Raj is a 29-year-old South Asian man who owns a small convenience store in a suburban neighborhood. He has been in a relationship with his partner, Anika, for four years, and they live together. He presents with a guarded posture, often avoiding eye contact when speaking about his home life. He is neatly dressed, but his hands tremble slightly as he adjusts his glasses, a gesture he repeats throughout our sessions.

The traumatic event occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Raj describes a night that began like many others: Anika had come home late from work, and they argued about finances. He does not recall the exact words exchanged, only the escalation. He remembers her hand connecting with his cheek, the shock of it, and then the sustained beating. He was pinned against the kitchen counter, her fists landing on his ribs, his back, his face. He did not fight back. He says, "I just took it. I thought if I stayed still, it would stop." It did stop, but only after he had curled into a ball on the tile floor. He did not call the police. He did not go to the hospital. The next morning, he told his customers he had fallen down the stairs.

In the months that followed, Raj's life constricted. He stopped inviting friends over. He began closing his shop an hour early, claiming he was tired. In truth, he could not bear the drive home in the dark. The headlights of oncoming cars would trigger a visceral startle response-a sudden jerk of the steering wheel, a cold sweat. He now takes back roads, adding twenty minutes to his commute, to avoid the main street where the car headlights feel like searchlights.

His sleep is fragmented. He wakes at 3:17 AM every night, the exact time he estimates the beating ended. He lies rigid in bed, listening to Anika's breathing, hypervigilant for any shift in her sleep pattern. He has not slept in the same bed for three months. He sleeps on the couch, but even there, he keeps one arm draped over the armrest, as if ready to spring up. The hypervigilance extends to the shop. He has installed three extra security cameras, not for theft, but to monitor the door. He describes a constant, low-grade dread-a feeling that something terrible is about to happen, even on quiet afternoons when the bell above the door doesn't ring.

He avoids conflict at all costs. A customer's complaint about a price sends his heart racing. He apologizes profusely, gives them a discount, and then retreats to the back room, shaking. He has stopped watching any movie or TV show with even a hint of domestic tension. The other day, a child dropped a glass bottle in the aisle. The sound of shattering glass sent him to his knees behind the counter, his breath coming in short, ragged gasps. He told the child's mother it was fine, he was just tired.

He carries a profound, unspoken shame. He believes that as a man, he should have been able to stop it. He has not told his family. He has not told his friends. He fears being seen as weak, or worse, being blamed. He says, "In our culture, a man is supposed to be the protector. I couldn't even protect myself." He has started to withdraw from Anika emotionally, not out of anger, but out of a deep, paralyzing fear that her affection is a prelude to another attack. He cannot differentiate between her gentle touch and the grip of her hand that night. He feels trapped, not by her, but by the memory of what happened, a memory that replays in his mind with the same clarity, the same sound of his own ribs cracking, every single day. He came to therapy not because he wants to leave, but because he is exhausted from the constant, silent war inside his own body.
